name: Pedro Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do management and accounting, so it's lectures in the morning, a bus to the flat I share with a guy from my course, and then a dinner shift at a pizzeria on Friday and Saturday. I wash dishes and sometimes do the till. My dad runs a small restaurant back home, Haddad's Kitchen, and I want to do its books one day. I like paper. I keep a notebook for everything and I don't use any AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, about time somebody said it. I've seen enough shiny things that didn't change much. At the pizzeria they've got a tablet for orders and it still breaks every Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine on the AI side. My worry is the usual stuff: my dad's restaurant had a bad winter, food costs are up, and the family helps me with rent and some of the fees. If his takings fall, the help falls too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working my two shifts, study the accounting modules properly, and start doing small jobs for my dad's books in the holidays. I'd keep saving about 50 a month in a tin, an actual tin. Nothing fancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. Not happy, not sad. Like a normal Tuesday. A bit tired, because the pizzeria shifts end at midnight and I've got a nine o'clock lecture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the family help depends on your dad's takings. How close is that to the edge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Close enough that I watch it. If a month goes badly, Dad doesn't tell me, but Mum mentions that he's skipped the new fridge. That's how I know. I'd rather earn more at the pizzeria than ask my parents for the 200 they send.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the tin teach you that a bank doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That cash is real. I put 50 in, and I can shake it and hear it. I know it sounds old, but a number on a screen feels like it could change. I'd use the bank for the big stuff, but the tin is mine.

say: I'd say **about time** somebody called it hype.
I'd mention that the pizzeria's order **tablet** still breaks every Friday night.
think: The AI side is fine; the real worry is **Dad's takings**.
If the restaurant has a bad winter, my **rent help** falls.
do: **Keep** the Friday and Saturday pizzeria shifts.
**Do** small bookkeeping jobs for Dad's restaurant in the holidays.
feel: **Tired** from midnight shifts before nine o'clock lectures.
S0.quote: I'd rather earn more at the pizzeria than ask my parents for the 200 they send.
fieldNote: Plain-spoken and **practical**; no appetite for hype or panic.
His real anxiety is the family restaurant's thin margins, not AI.
Notes that cash in a tin feels real; screens feel changeable.

steps.text: Keep washing dishes at the pizzeria on Fridays and Saturdays
Put 50 a month into the savings tin
Do Dad's restaurant books during the holidays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's worrying for office jobs and I'd want to see it before I believe it. Accounting is checking numbers, and that's what these tools do. But I'd also say firms still need someone to sign the thing and take the blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm nervous. Everything in my first-year modules, like ledgers, reconciliations and tax forms, is the checking and booking work they said would go first. I don't want to be the junior who sits at a desk while the software does his job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay away from the new tools for now, which my friends say is stubborn. I'd go to the careers talk, ask my tutors what they use, and probably try one in third year if it's proven. I'd also learn how a restaurant's books really work from Dad, because small businesses are slower to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense. Like waiting for a result. I'm not panicking, but I feel it when I look at the textbook and think this might be the part that goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait until a tool is proven. What counts as proven for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When two or three people I trust, like my tutor or my cousin who works at an accountancy firm, say it works and doesn't make mistakes. I'm not against it. I just don't like being first and finding the mistake at tax time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a classmate who says you're falling behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm learning the basics so I can tell when the tool is wrong. A person who can't do a bank reconciliation by hand can't check one. I don't think slow is the same as behind, but I know that's easy to say.

say: I'd say **accounting** is checking numbers, and that's what the tools do.
I'd say firms still need someone to **sign** and take blame.
think: My first-year **ledgers** are the checking work said to go first.
I don't want to be the **junior** whose job the software does.
do: **Ask** tutors which tools firms actually use.
**Learn** a restaurant's real books from Dad.
**Try** one proven tool in third year.
feel: **Not panicking**, but uneasy at the textbook.
S1.quote: A person who can't do a bank reconciliation by hand can't check one.
fieldNote: Resistance is **reasoned**: he wants proof from people he trusts before he tries a tool.
His chosen field is exactly the checking work that the card says goes first.
Has a family business as a fallback and a source of learning.

steps.text: Ask my tutors which tools accountancy firms use
Learn how a restaurant's books work from Dad
Wait for trusted people to vouch before trying a tool
Add a small business bookkeeping module next term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it, and if it's true then nobody's ready. Two years is nothing. I'd say it quietly to my friends and not post anything, because I wouldn't know what to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. I'm in the middle of a degree that's meant to train me for work they say will be done by machines in two years. Dad's restaurant would still stand until the robots come in 2031, but his customers might lose their jobs and stop eating out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the pizzeria job, because it's hands-on and it pays. I'd probably go home more often and help in Dad's kitchen, learning to cook and to run the place, because that's something I can hold on to. And I'd ask the uni whether I could change to something like hospitality management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground's gone soft. I'd keep doing normal things, like going to class, but I'd have trouble caring about an essay on tax law.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the customers might stop eating out. Walk me through that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If office people lose work, they cut the small treats first, like Friday dinners. The restaurant lives off office lunches and family birthdays. If that dips for a year, Dad has to choose between paying staff and paying himself, and he always picks the staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for your dad then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take a year out, if I had to, and work in the kitchen full time for free. It's not a plan I'd boast about, but family first. I wouldn't ask anyone's permission, I'd just turn up and put on an apron.

say: I'd say **nobody is ready** and keep it quiet with friends.
I'd **not post** anything, because I wouldn't know what to say.
think: My degree may train me for work **machines** take in two years.
If office workers lose jobs, **Dad's restaurant** loses its lunches.
do: **Keep** the pizzeria job because it's hands-on and pays.
**Go home** more to learn Dad's kitchen and its running.
**Ask** the uni about switching to hospitality management.
feel: The ground feels **soft** under my feet.
I'd struggle to **care** about a tax law essay.
S2.quote: If office people lose work, they cut the small treats first, like Friday dinners.
fieldNote: Reaches for **family and hands-on work** as the anchor.
Links his father's restaurant to the office economy, which shows real thought.
Would give up a year of study for his dad without being asked.

steps.text: Keep the pizzeria job through the first year
Go home most weekends to learn Dad's kitchen
Ask the university about hospitality management
Talk to Mum about what the family can still afford

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to think and not enough to relax. I'd tell friends to stop assuming it's only other people's jobs. I'd say it in a calm way, because shouting doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'm just graduating. That's the worst moment. But I'd have my degree, and a family business, and I think that gives me a small edge over someone with only a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and work summers in the restaurant's front office, changing the way it keeps books. If the tools turned out to be proven by 2029, I'd learn one, slowly. I'd also save about 80 a month, and push Dad to put some aside, because bad luck usually comes in pairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weighed down, but able to move. Like carrying a bag of flour. Heavy, but I can still walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd push your dad to save. How does a conversation like that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, at first. He says a restaurant is a business of today and he's proud. But I'd show him a notebook with the numbers for a bad month, and he'd read it. He respects paper. Mum would side with me, and that would settle it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good outcome look like for you in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A job at a small firm that does accounts for local shops, where people still want to sit across a desk from someone they know. And Dad's place still open on Saturdays with my name on the books. That would be enough.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to think**, not to relax.
I'd say it **calmly**, because shouting doesn't help.
think: Five years means I **graduate** at the worst moment.
A degree plus a **family business** gives me a small edge.
do: **Finish** the degree and work summers in the restaurant office.
**Save** 80 a month and push Dad to save too.
feel: **Weighed down**, like carrying a bag of flour.
Still **able to walk**, so not stuck.
S3.quote: A job at a small firm that does accounts for local shops, where people still want to sit across a desk from someone they know.
fieldNote: Builds a **small, local** picture of success rather than chasing big firms.
Expects to win Dad round with numbers on paper, which fits his style.
Anxious because graduation and the change arrive together.

steps.text: Work summers in the restaurant's front office
Save 80 a month from the pizzeria wages
Learn one accounting tool if proven by 2029
Finish the accounting degree on schedule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long time and people shouldn't panic. I'd say it to my dad, mostly, who worries more than he lets on. I'd also say we should be sensible and build a few things that last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be quite okay. By 2036 I'd be 28 with ten years of work behind me, maybe a small firm of my own. Ten years is enough to change my mind about the tools, which I'd probably do once they're everywhere and boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work at a regional accountancy, and put money aside every month. I'd help Dad modernise the restaurant slowly, like online bookings, one step at a time. And once the tools are proven I'd learn them, in my late twenties, without fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a long drive on a straight road. You can see the end, and you're allowed to stop for coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd change your mind once they are boring. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen people burned by the first version of everything. The restaurant got a booking app in 2023 that double-booked tables for months. Waiting for the second version isn't being scared, it's being careful with someone else's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you in a ten-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clear information, in plain language, from someone with no stake. I don't want a sales video. I want an accountant my age who's actually used it, telling me what it's good for. Ten years gives enough time for that to turn up.

say: I'd say **don't panic**; build things that last.
I'd tell **Dad**, who worries more than he lets on.
think: By 2036 I'd be **28** with ten years of work behind me.
Ten years is enough to change my mind about **tools** once they're boring.
do: **Finish** the degree and join a regional accountancy.
**Modernise** Dad's restaurant slowly, starting with online bookings.
**Learn** proven tools in my late twenties.
feel: **Calm**, like a long drive on a straight road.
Allowed to **stop for coffee**, meaning time to wait.
S4.quote: Waiting for the second version isn't being scared, it's being careful with someone else's money.
fieldNote: His **resistance** has a reason: a double-booking app that burned the family.
Time lets him step towards the tools without losing face.
Looks for plain advice from a peer, not a sales pitch.

steps.text: Finish the degree and join a regional accountancy
Help Dad add online bookings to the restaurant
Learn the tools only after others have proven them
Put 100 a month aside from my first salary

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'd have no time to finish my degree before the work I'm training for is done by machines, and Dad's restaurant would take the knock from people losing office jobs. What would help is clear information and a safety net so a family business doesn't fold over one bad year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against new things, I'm against being first, and the careful ones often still have their savings. I'd like people to stop calling that being stubborn.

headlineQuote: I'm not against new things, I'm against being first, and the careful ones often still have their savings.
portrait: Pedro is an **18-year-old** accounting and management student who washes dishes at a pizzeria on weekends.
He keeps paper notebooks, a savings tin and **never uses AI**, wanting proof from trusted people first.
His outlook is **centre**: practical, unshowy and more interested in what works than in who is right.
The family **restaurant** is his anchor and his worry; a bad year there cuts his rent help.
He moves from steady in the quiet world to alarm at 2028, then calm when ten years allows cautious learning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his degree and his father's restaurant would both be hit with no time.
whatWouldHelp: A **safety net** so a family business doesn't fold over one bad year.
**Plain information** from people who have used the tools.
